newsitem.title: USA: No quarantine yet for Tennessee karnal bunt wheat.
newsitem.headline: No quarantine yet for Tennessee karnal bunt wheat.

text.p: The Tennessee Department of Agriculture is taking extraordinary measures to control the spread of karnal bunt fungus but no quarantine has been imposed yet, said spokesman Tom Womack.
"It would be too early to talk about a quarantine," Womack said. "We really won't know until we have a meeting with USDA as to whether we will have a quarantine as such."
He added the state agriculture department will meet with USDA "in the next 24 to 48 hours."
Karnal bunt fungus was detected in soft red winter wheat grown in one Tennessee county and is suspected in wheat from at least six others, Womack said.
In a letter to the USDA, Tennessee Governor Don Sundquist asked that "extraordinary emergency measures be taken," according to a news release issued Thursday.

Those measures include disposing of the contaminated wheat, sanitizing wheat storage facilities, establishing a regular monitoring and testing program and securing federal funds to compensate farmers for losses, the release states.

"State and federal officials will be working closely with farmers and grain warehouse operators to properly dispose of contaminated grain and to provide options for cleaning and sanitizing storage facilities," the release said.
Tennessee farmers harvested an estimated 17.6 million bushels of wheat in 1996. About 95 percent of that was soft red winter wheat, Womack said.

USDA has been testing for karnal bunt across the country since it was discovered in March in Arizona. The fungus, named after a town in India where is was first discovered, has also been found in New Mexico, Texas, California and Alabama.
Karnal bunt does not pose a health risk to humans but can lower crop yields. Flour made from bunted kernels is often discolored and has an unpleasant odor and taste.
